html:
A long war in the dry lands north of central Mexico, from 1550 into the 1590s, between Spain and the nomadic and farming peoples the Spaniards lumped together as Chichimecas. It was the longest and most costly war Spain fought against Native peoples in North America.

It began after silver was found at Zacatecas in 1546. A road was cut north from Mexico City to the mines, through the lands of the Guachichiles, Zacatecos, Guamares and Pames. These peoples raided the wagon trains and mining camps, using bows with great skill. The fighting followed on from the Mixtón War of 1540 to 1542.

Spain first tried "war by fire and blood": forts, soldiers, and selling captives as slaves. It did not work. In the 1580s and 1590s the viceroyalty of New Spain switched to "peace by purchase". It gave food, clothing and tools, sent missionaries, and settled Tlaxcalan and Otomí families in new towns among the Chichimecas as models and buffers. The raids died away.

The peace opened the north to silver mining and ranching. Over time the Chichimeca peoples were mostly absorbed or died out from disease, though the Pames and Chichimeca Jonaz survive.
